ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Younger adults (n = 172; Mage = 23.7, SD = 3.8, range 18-35; 133 women, 39 men) and older adults (n = 174; Mage = 71.5, SD = 4.3, range 65-80; 97 women, 77 men) were recruited from the Zurich area (younger adults: university students; older adults: from the community).
All participants provided written informed consent and were debriefed in the end.
In the individual differences study, participants completed a battery of 21 tasks, nine of which are reported here.
Participants completed a color matching and an orientation matching task with 50 trials each.

A probe was presented 200 pixels right of center, and participants had to adjust the probe's feature by moving the mouse cursor along a 360° color wheel (CIELAB, L* = 70, a* = 20, b* = 38, radius = 60), as used by Zhang and Luck (2008), or by rotating the probe over its axis (see Figure 1 for an illustration).
table.formatted: A probe was presented 200 pixels right of center, and participants had to adjust the probe's feature by moving the mouse cursor along a 360° color wheel (CIELAB, L* = 70, a* = 20, b* = 38, radius = 60), as used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Zhang and Luck (2008)</ref>, or by rotating the probe over its axis (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> for an illustration).

table.text: Participants completed a color and an orientation delayed estimation (DE) task with 100 trials each.
Participants had to identify the one non-conforming sequence.
For each item, participants had to select the piece that correctly completes a figural matrix pattern both row-and column-wise from a set of eight alternatives.

Younger adults (N = 267; Mage = 23.0, SD = 3.6, range 18-35; 179 women, 80 men, 1 non-binary) were recruited via an online job market and mailing lists and received CHF 200 for the full study or partial course credit if they were students.
All participants provided written informed consent.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Younger adults (n = 172; Mage = 23.7, SD = 3.8, range 18-35; 133 women, 39 men) and older adults (n = 174; Mage = 71.5, SD = 4.3, range 65-80; 97 women, 77 men) were recruited from the Zurich area (younger adults: university students; older adults: from the community).

> All participants provided written informed consent and were debriefed in the end.

> In the individual differences study, participants completed a battery of 21 tasks, nine of which are reported here.

> Participants completed a color matching and an orientation matching task with 50 trials each.

> A probe was presented 200 pixels right of center, and participants had to adjust the probe's feature by moving the mouse cursor along a 360° color wheel (CIELAB, L* = 70, a* = 20, b* = 38, radius = 60), as used by Zhang and Luck (2008), or by rotating the probe over its axis (see Figure 1 for an illustration).

> Participants completed a color and an orientation delayed estimation (DE) task with 100 trials each.

> Participants had to identify the one non-conforming sequence.

> For each item, participants had to select the piece that correctly completes a figural matrix pattern both row-and column-wise from a set of eight alternatives.

> Younger adults (N = 267; Mage = 23.0, SD = 3.6, range 18-35; 179 women, 80 men, 1 non-binary) were recruited via an online job market and mailing lists and received CHF 200 for the full study or partial course credit if they were students.

> All participants provided written informed consent.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

codebook_check.title: Codebook Check
codebook_check.summary_text: We found no codebook or README documentation for the 955 extracted data columns.
report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 66 codebook/README/label sources and 955 data columns across 82 files.
No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.
#### Duplicated Column Names

- **Duplicated column names in `CorrTable_Baseline.csv`.** 2 column names appear more than once (worst: `0.28`×2, `0.44`×2), so 4 of the file's 14 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

-  We could not classify 112 files.
-  The manuscript's studies and the repository's file groups do not match.
-  We found 687 file naming problems to fix.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 7 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (1), R history (6). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1311 columns across 103 data files.
#### Issues Identified

30 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 103 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Younger adults (n = 172; Mage = 23.7, SD = 3.8, range 18-35; 133 women, 39 men) and older adults (n = 174; Mage = 71.5, SD = 4.3, range 65-80; 97 women, 77 men) were recruited from the Zurich area (younger adults: university students; older adults: from the community).
All participants provided written informed consent and were debriefed in the end.
In the individual differences study, participants completed a battery of 21 tasks, nine of which are reported here.
Participants completed a color matching and an orientation matching task with 50 trials each.

A probe was presented 200 pixels right of center, and participants had to adjust the probe's feature by moving the mouse cursor along a 360° color wheel (CIELAB, L* = 70, a* = 20, b* = 38, radius = 60), as used by Zhang and Luck (2008), or by rotating the probe over its axis (see Figure 1 for an illustration).
Participants completed a color and an orientation delayed estimation (DE) task with 100 trials each.
Participants had to identify the one non-conforming sequence.
For each item, participants had to select the piece that correctly completes a figural matrix pattern both row-and column-wise from a set of eight alternatives.

Younger adults (N = 267; Mage = 23.0, SD = 3.6, range 18-35; 179 women, 80 men, 1 non-binary) were recruited via an online job market and mailing lists and received CHF 200 for the full study or partial course credit if they were students.
All participants provided written informed consent.

#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 92 scripts: 6 ran without error, 19 errored, 0 timed out, 30 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 20 were run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script needs the internet**, which is off during the run: 10_public_data_reanalysis.R. **`setwd()` in the code**
**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Analysis_AgeDifferences.R", "setwd() removed" = 1L, 
    "Path(s) it set" = "(non-literal)"), row.names = c(NA, -1L
), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**
14 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

keywords: and Writing -review & editing. Klaus Oberauer: conceptualization
and Writing -review & editing. Alessandra Souza: investigation

text.text: Working memory capacity (WMC) and fluid intelligence (Gf) are strongly correlated, usually attributed to shared demands on WM maintenance.
We test this account against an alternative: shared representational quality.
We included an experimentally controlled simplification of visual WM tasks -a perceptual matching task without maintenance demands -alongside WMC and Gf measures.
Study 1 (N = 346; younger and older adults) used color and orientation stimuli; Study 2 (N = 267; younger adults) added luminance matching and a broader WMC battery.
Matching accuracy strongly predicted Gf and accounted for a large share of the WMC-Gf covariance.
WM maintenance accounted for unique Gf variance over and above matching in all groups.
These findings are consistent with a shared signal-to-noise ratio affecting perceptual discrimination, WMC, and Gf.
They question the view that the WMC-Gf relationship reflects only demands on WM maintenance, while confirming a specific role of maintenance for Gf.

Working memory capacity (WMC), our ability to keep information accessible in mind for ongoing cognition, is among the strongest correlates of fluid intelligence (Gf; Kyllonen & Christal, 1990; Ackerman et al., 2005; Oberauer et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Working memory capacity (WMC), our ability to keep information accessible in mind for ongoing cognition, is among the strongest correlates of fluid intelligence (Gf; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Kyllonen & Christal, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Ackerman et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Oberauer et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Latent correlations between WMC and Gf frequently approach unity across diverse task batteries, pointing to common processes responsible for individual differences in both (Conway & Kovacs, 2020; Wilhelm et al., 2013 Wilhelm et al., , 2025)).
text.formatted: Latent correlations between WMC and Gf frequently approach unity across diverse task batteries, pointing to common processes responsible for individual differences in both <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Conway & Kovacs, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wilhelm et al., 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Wilhelm et al., , 2025))</ref>.

text.text: Identifying these common processes is critical for understanding what fundamentally limits cognitive performance.
Working memory (WM) theorists differ on what they consider to be limited in WMC, but they all support the view that maintenance functions are critical to explain the WMC-Gf link.
Binding and storage accounts argue that WMC limits are specific to the temporary integration of information into memory representations (Oberauer et al., 2003; Süß et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Binding and storage accounts argue that WMC limits are specific to the temporary integration of information into memory representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Oberauer et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Süß et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Attentional control accounts emphasize executive processes that shield WM representations against interference (Engle, 2002).
text.formatted: Attentional control accounts emphasize executive processes that shield WM representations against interference <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Engle, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Yet establishing whether maintenance specifically drives the WMC-Gf link requires control conditions that isolate contributions from perceptual factors separately from storage demands, controls that WM research has largely neglected.

Some recent results questioned the role of WM maintenance for individual differences in WMC. Pratte and Green (2023) showed that individual differences in visual WM are largely paralleled by variations in sensory memory.
text.formatted: Some recent results questioned the role of WM maintenance for individual differences in WMC. <ref type="bibr">Pratte and Green (2023)</ref> showed that individual differences in visual WM are largely paralleled by variations in sensory memory.

text.text: A limitation of that study is that sensory memory tests involved briefly maintaining multiple representations simultaneously, which may rely on WMC.
Prior studies on sensory discrimination ability found that it shares substantial variance with Gf and WMC.

This was observed with sequential designs for measuring sensory discrimination, in which the first stimulus must be held in memory while the second is processed (Troche et al., 2014), and with briefly presented simultaneous stimulus pairs (Jastrzębski et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This was observed with sequential designs for measuring sensory discrimination, in which the first stimulus must be held in memory while the second is processed <ref type="bibr">(Troche et al., 2014)</ref>, and with briefly presented simultaneous stimulus pairs <ref type="bibr">(Jastrzębski et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These studies further tested whether discrimination predicts Gf beyond WMC and found that WMC fully mediated the discrimination-Gf covariation; however, they did not decompose the WMC-Gf covariance itself and estimate how much of the WMC-Gf covariance is shared with purely perceptual tasks.
These findings suggest that the WMC-Gf link may trace to a basic property of both perceptual and non-perceptual representations rather than to maintenance-specific demands.
Converging evidence supports this possibility.
In aging research, visual and auditory acuity accounted for 49% of total and 93% of age-related variance in intelligence (Lindenberger & Baltes, 1994), suggesting a common neural substrate.
text.formatted: In aging research, visual and auditory acuity accounted for 49% of total and 93% of age-related variance in intelligence <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lindenberger & Baltes, 1994)</ref>, suggesting a common neural substrate.

text.text: This could be explained by age-related reductions in dopaminergic neuromodulation, which increase cortical noise, simultaneously degrading perceptual discrimination and higher cognitive functions including WM (Li et al., 2001).
text.formatted: This could be explained by age-related reductions in dopaminergic neuromodulation, which increase cortical noise, simultaneously degrading perceptual discrimination and higher cognitive functions including WM <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Li et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: The recently proposed signal-to-noise ratio hypothesis of general intelligence (SNR-g; Oberauer et al., 2026) develops this account further: A global signal-to-noise ratio of neural processing constrains performance across perceptual and non-perceptual tasks alike, producing the positive manifold of cognitive abilities.
text.formatted: The recently proposed signal-to-noise ratio hypothesis of general intelligence (SNR-g; <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Oberauer et al., 2026)</ref> develops this account further: A global signal-to-noise ratio of neural processing constrains performance across perceptual and non-perceptual tasks alike, producing the positive manifold of cognitive abilities.

text.text: The aim of this study is to decompose the shared variance between WMC and Gf into a component reflecting WM maintenance and a component reflecting the formation of precise stimulus representations.

To do so, we designed a perceptual-matching task to measure perceptual precision through an experimental simplification of a well-established task for measuring visual WMC (i.e., delayed estimation, DE), removing only the demand to maintain information no longer perceptually available.

With this design we can decompose the variance in Gf into four components: (1) the variance shared between Gf, WMC as measured by delayed estimation (WMCDE), and perceptual matching; (2) the Gf variance shared only with WMCDE; (3) the Gf variance shared only with perceptual matching; and (4) the residual Gf variance not shared with either predictor.
The maintenance account of the Gf-WMC relationship predicts a large component shared between Gf and WMCDE only and a small component shared with both predictors.
Conversely, the signal-to-noise-ratio account predicts a large component shared by Gf, WMCDE, and perceptual matching.
By our experimental design, the delayed estimation task makes the same demands as the perceptual matching task plus maintenance.
Therefore, we predict that the component capturing variance uniquely shared between Gf and perceptual matching should be near zero.
This is the full-mediation pattern that prior studies interpreted as ruling out a perceptual contribution to intelligence.

Study 2 was supported by the Swiss National Science Foundation under Ambizione Grant PZ00P1_208828 to Gidon T. Frischkorn.

Klaus Oberauer was supported by Swiss National Science Foundation Grant 10531CL_219765.1 Prior studies used sensory discrimination tasks which involved comparing two stimuli and deciding if they were the same or selecting the one with the larger value.
Here we used a perceptual matching task requiring participants to adjust a stimulus to be of the same value (e.g., same color, orientation, or brightness) as a visible target.
We assume both classes of tasks measure the same construct, namely the precision of sensory traces.
Study 1 used data from a large individual differences study on age differences in the ability to focus attention (Souza et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Study 1 used data from a large individual differences study on age differences in the ability to focus attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Souza et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Younger adults (n = 172; Mage = 23.7, SD = 3.8, range 18-35; 133 women, 39 men) and older adults (n = 174; Mage = 71.5, SD = 4.3, range 65-80; 97 women, 77 men) were recruited from the Zurich area (younger adults: university students; older adults: from the community).
Participants received 15 Swiss francs (ca.
16 US dollars) per hour, or, for students, partial course credit.
All participants provided written informed consent and were debriefed in the end.
In the individual differences study, participants completed a battery of 21 tasks, nine of which are reported here.
Data from two of the nine tasks (Color and Orientation DE) were previously published but with a focus on different results (Souza et al., 2024; Souza & Frischkorn, 2023).
text.formatted: Data from two of the nine tasks (Color and Orientation DE) were previously published but with a focus on different results <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Souza et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Souza & Frischkorn, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Perceptual Matching Tasks.
Participants completed a color matching and an orientation matching task with 50 trials each.
On each trial, a target (colored circle or oriented triangle) was presented 200 pixels left of the screen center.

A probe was presented 200 pixels right of center, and participants had to adjust the probe's feature by moving the mouse cursor along a 360° color wheel (CIELAB, L* = 70, a* = 20, b* = 38, radius = 60), as used by Zhang and Luck (2008), or by rotating the probe over its axis (see Figure 1 for an illustration).
text.formatted: A probe was presented 200 pixels right of center, and participants had to adjust the probe's feature by moving the mouse cursor along a 360° color wheel (CIELAB, L* = 70, a* = 20, b* = 38, radius = 60), as used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Zhang and Luck (2008)</ref>, or by rotating the probe over its axis (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> for an illustration).

text.text: To maximize the exploration of the feature space, target values were sampled with a minimum distance of 5° between them.
Performance was quantified as the angular distance between the response and the correct target feature value.

We computed the mean angular error across trials for each participant and rescaled it to an accuracy score: 100 × (1 -mean angular error / 90°), yielding a 0-100 scale where higher values reflect greater accuracy.
Participants completed a color and an orientation delayed estimation (DE) task with 100 trials each.

On each trial, an array of colored circles (color DE) or oriented triangles (orientation DE) was presented for a 1000 ms, followed by a 1,000 ms blank retention interval, after which participants reproduced the color or orientation of a randomly selected probed item (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: On each trial, an array of colored circles (color DE) or oriented triangles (orientation DE) was presented for a 1000 ms, followed by a 1,000 ms blank retention interval, after which participants reproduced the color or orientation of a randomly selected probed item (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: In 50% of trials, a retro-cue indicated the probed item prior to the test; the present analyses use only the 50 no-cue trials of each task.
Memory load was determined by a pilot calibration aimed at comparable difficulty between age groups.
Color DE included two loads per group (younger adults: 5 and 6 items; older adults: 4 and 5 items); orientation DE used a single load per group (younger: 6 items; older: 4 items).
Performance was quantified in the same manner as described for the matching tasks (see Souza et al., 2024 for full task details).
text.formatted: Performance was quantified in the same manner as described for the matching tasks (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Souza et al., 2024</ref> for full task details).

text.text: To anchor our findings on established psychometric measures of WMC, we used two tasks from the Working Memory Battery by Lewandowsky et al. (2010).
text.formatted: To anchor our findings on established psychometric measures of WMC, we used two tasks from the Working Memory Battery by <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Lewandowsky et al. (2010)</ref>.

text.text: In the Spatial Short-Term Memory task (SSTM), participants viewed 2-6 dots appearing one by one in cells of a 10 × 10 grid and reproduced the Note.
In the matching task (Panel A), the target (left) remains visible while participants adjust the probe (right) on a continuous scale (a 360° color wheel or by rotating the triangle).

In the delayed estimation task (Panel B), the memory array was shown for 1 s, followed by 1-s blank retention interval; participants adjusted the feature of a randomly selected probe at the end of the trial (untimed).
The angular distance between the response and the probed item's original feature is the response error.
remembered spatial pattern by clicking the corresponding cells (30 trials; scored as the percentage match between original and reproduced pattern after optimal alignment).

In the Memory Updating task, participants encoded an initial set of 3-5 digits that appeared across a set of frames, then they updated their values via a series of arithmetic operations (2-6 steps per trial; 15 trials total) and finally were prompted to type the final digit in each frame.
Performance was scored as the percentage of correctly recalled final digits.

Participants' Gf was measured with three time-restricted reasoning tests: In the Letter Sets task (Ekstrom et al., 1976), participants worked on 30 items in two parts with a time limit of 7 min for each part.
text.formatted: Participants' Gf was measured with three time-restricted reasoning tests: In the Letter Sets task <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Ekstrom et al., 1976)</ref>, participants worked on 30 items in two parts with a time limit of 7 min for each part.

text.text: Each item consisted of five four-letter sequences, of which four shared a common abstract logical rule.
Participants had to identify the one non-conforming sequence.
In the short version of Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices (Arthur et al., 1999), participants worked on 12 items with a time limit of 15 min.
text.formatted: In the short version of Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Arthur et al., 1999)</ref>, participants worked on 12 items with a time limit of 15 min.

text.text: For each item, participants had to select the piece that correctly completes a figural matrix pattern both row-and column-wise from a set of eight alternatives.

In the Diagramming Relationships task (Ekstrom et al., 1976), participants worked on 30 items in two parts, with a time limit of 4 min each, and had to select which of five Venn diagrams correctly represents the set-membership relations among three named categories.
text.formatted: In the Diagramming Relationships task <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Ekstrom et al., 1976)</ref>, participants worked on 30 items in two parts, with a time limit of 4 min each, and had to select which of five Venn diagrams correctly represents the set-membership relations among three named categories.

text.text: Performance was scored as the percentage of correct items in each test.

To test whether the WMC-Gf relationship traces to representational quality rather than maintenance in WM, we used latent-variable structural equation modeling (SEM) to estimate (a) the zero-order latent correlations of Matching accuracy and WMC with Gf, (b) how much WMC-Gf covariance persists after removing variance shared with Matching accuracy, and (c) how much Gf-predictive variance Matching retains beyond WMC.

WMC was operationalized through two factors: one reflecting performance in delayed estimation tasks (the WMCDE factor) and one reflecting performance on traditional psychometric tasks (the WMCPM factor).
The WMCDE factor captures variance shared with the continuous-report format of the perceptual matching tasks but adds the encoding and maintenance of multiple items across a retention interval.

The matching tasks are thus an experimentally controlled simplification of the DE tasks using identical stimuli and response format, with the maintenance requirement and the multipleitem load removed.
Hence, the processes required by Matching form a subset of those required by DE, whereas the DE factor adds a maintenance-dependent counterpart to Matching.

The WMCPM factor additionally captures maintenance ability for spatial and numerical material and represents a more far-reaching relation of Matching to WMC tests with different stimuli and response formats.
Models were fit with Bayesian estimation using the blavaan R package (Merkle et al., 2021), with standardized latent variances.
text.formatted: Models were fit with Bayesian estimation using the blavaan R package <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Merkle et al., 2021)</ref>, with standardized latent variances.

text.text: Each model was estimated with four MCMC chains of 10,000 post-warmup iterations; convergence was excellent for all reported models (all !

We used weakly informative priors for the measurement and structural parameters, and the residual correlations tested for incremental validity received a stretched-beta prior (' = ) = 3), equivalent to the default "medium" width prior of Bayesian correlation tests.
Missing data were handled through full-information (casewise) likelihood, so all participants contributed to every model.
We report standardized parameters as posterior medians with 95% credible intervals (CrI).
Model fit was evaluated with the posterior predictive p value (PPP) and Bayesian analogues of the CFI and RMSEA (BCFI, BRMSEA; Garnier-Villarreal & Jorgensen, 2020).
text.formatted: Model fit was evaluated with the posterior predictive p value (PPP) and Bayesian analogues of the CFI and RMSEA (BCFI, BRMSEA; Garnier-Villarreal & Jorgensen, 2020).

text.text: To capture variance specific to each feature domain without contaminating the general accuracy factors used in the residual and reverse-residual tests, we specified bifactor models with one domain-specific factor per task × feature-domain combination (e.g., color matching, color DE), orthogonal to the general factors (see the detailed model specifications in the online supplement).

A domain-specific factor lives inside a single task, so it cannot absorb variance shared across tasks; that is the job of the freely estimated within-domain covariances (color matching with color DE; orientation matching with orientation DE), which capture stimulus-content variance shared between matching and DE beyond what the general factors already explain.

The two are therefore not redundant: domain-specific factors absorb task-bound variance -response-format idiosyncrasies and stimulus-content variance unique to that task -while within-domain covariances absorb the stimulus-content variance shared across tasks, keeping the general-factor correlations from being inflated by that shared method variance.

Factor reliabilities are reported as hierarchical McDonald's omega (ωH), that is the proportion of variance in a factor's indicators that is attributable to that factor, excluding these reliable domain-specific components, computed per posterior draw from the correlation-model posteriors and summarized as posterior medians.
text.formatted: Factor reliabilities are reported as hierarchical <ref type="bibr">McDonald's omega (ωH)</ref>, that is the proportion of variance in a factor's indicators that is attributable to that factor, excluding these reliable domain-specific components, computed per posterior draw from the correlation-model posteriors and summarized as posterior medians.

text.text: To account for measurement error, task performance was summarized via three trial-split parcels in the matching and DE tasks, which serve as observed indicators of the latent factors and provide a theoretically justified parallel-test structure.

Parcels were formed by cycling through trials in their presentation order and assigning every third trial to the same parcel (i.e., trials 1, 4, 7, … → parcel 1; trials 2, 5, 8, … → parcel 2; etc.), yielding approximately equal trial counts across parcels.

All task scores were coded so that higher values reflect better performance, and every indicator was expressed on a common 0-100 metric (matching and DE accuracy, and percentage correct for the WMC and reasoning tasks).

Placing the indicators on a comparable scale keeps their variances of similar magnitude and avoids the ill-conditioning that can destabilize SEM estimation when indicator variances differ by orders of magnitude; because this is a linear rescaling of each indicator, it leaves all standardized estimates unchanged.

We fit three structural models on the same measurement model: First, we estimated a zero-order correlation model with all general factors freely correlated, yielding zero-order latent correlations with Gf.

Second, we estimated a residual correlation model in which both the general factor for the WMCDE tasks and WMCPM measures were predicted by the Matching factor, yielding residual (partial) correlations of WMCDE and WMCPM with Gf after accounting for variance shared with Matching.

Third, we estimated the reverse residual model, in which the Matching factor was regressed on WMCDE (its maintenance-enriched counterpart) yielding the residual correlation of Matching with Gf after accounting for variance shared with WMCDE.

This third model is the latent-variable analogue of testing whether WMC fully mediates the relation between sensory discrimination and Gf (Jastrzębski et al., 2021; Troche et al., 2014); variants controlling for WMCPM instead of, or in addition to, WMCDE are reported in the Supplementary Materials.
text.formatted: This third model is the latent-variable analogue of testing whether WMC fully mediates the relation between sensory discrimination and Gf <ref type="bibr">(Jastrzębski et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Troche et al., 2014)</ref>; variants controlling for WMCPM instead of, or in addition to, WMCDE are reported in the Supplementary Materials.

text.text: All three structural models are reparameterizations of the same latent covariance structure and fit the data identically.
The logic of these models can be illustrated with a simple variance decomposition.

Because the matching tasks are experimental simplifications of DE tasks, scores of both WMCDE and Matching factors depend on the precision of perceptual encoding (+), whereas only WMCDE additionally depends on maintenance ability (,): where the 6 terms collect task-specific variance, and the components are treated as additive and independent for illustration.
Under this idealization, the variance of Matching that can carry a relation to Gf (the precision of perceptual encoding +) is contained within that of WMCDE (+ and maintenance ,).

The residual correlation model then isolates the Gf-relevant variance in ,, and the reverse residual model tests the containment structure itself: If Matching carries no Gf-relevant variance beyond +, its residual correlation with Gf should be zero, replicating the full-mediation pattern reported by prior studies.
The primary outcome from the first two models is the proportional reduction in explained

Gf variance: 1 -(; ()* + /; , + ), where ; , is the zero-order latent correlation and ; ()* is the semipartial correlation r(Gf, predictor | Match), that is, the correlation between Gf and the Matching-residualised factors of WMCDE and WMCPM, standardized using the predictor's total (not residual) variance.
Squaring this semi-partial gives the unique R² of the predictor for Gf over and above the variance shared with Matching, so the formula equals (shared R²)/(total R²), a variance-partitioning metric.

To quantify the uncertainty of this proportional reduction, we estimated 95% credible intervals (CrIs) from the joint posterior of the residual model: on each posterior draw, ; , and ; ()* were computed from the same draw of the model parameters (; , via path tracing), ensuring the reduction is estimated from paired ; , and ; ()* values.
For incremental validity tests, we report Savage-Dickey density ratios of the tested residual correlation at zero (Wagenmakers et al., 2010).
text.formatted: For incremental validity tests, we report Savage-Dickey density ratios of the tested residual correlation at zero <ref type="bibr">(Wagenmakers et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The ratio of prior to posterior density at zero approximates Bayes factors for the alternative hypothesis (FG -, ), which represents evidence for an incremental predictive path.
Its reciprocal approximates the BF for the null (FG ,-), the evidence for no increment.
BF between 1/3 and 3 are reported as inconclusive evidence; only values beyond these bounds are interpreted as support for the alternative or the null hypothesis.
The reverse residual models yield the complementary proportional reduction of the Matching-Gf relation after controlling for the WM factor(s), computed from paired posterior draws in the same way.

If Matching's Gf-relevant variance is a subset of the WM factors' Gfrelevant variance, controlling for the WM factors must reduce the Matching-Gf relation more strongly than controlling for Matching reduces the WMC-Gf relations.

We tested this order restriction on the posterior of the correlation model, in which all latent correlations share the same prior; the two directions of the contrast are thus exchangeable a priori, the predicted order has a prior probability of .50, and its Bayes factor (BForder) equals the posterior odds of the predicted order (Wetzels et al., 2010).
text.formatted: We tested this order restriction on the posterior of the correlation model, in which all latent correlations share the same prior; the two directions of the contrast are thus exchangeable a priori, the predicted order has a prior probability of .50, and its Bayes factor (BForder) equals the posterior odds of the predicted order <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Wetzels et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: All analyses were repeated with rank-normalized indicators to check robustness to distributional assumptions, with a pure Gf factor for older adults to control for potential criterion contamination (as explained in the Results section), and with flatter priors on the tested residual correlations, to check robustness to prior choice; results were consistent across all analyses (see Supplemental Materials).
SEM were estimated separately for younger and older adults.

To stabilize estimation, the measurement model applied parallel-test constraints (equal loadings and error variances within each parcel bundle), which are theoretically justified for random trial-split parcels and were supported empirically: Approximate leave-one-out cross-validation favored the constrained over the unconstrained measurement model in both groups (ΔLOOIC = -23 for younger and -49 for older adults; negative values favor the constrained model).
Before comparing groups, we tested measurement invariance across younger and older adults using the standard configural, metric, and scalar sequence.

Configural and metric invariance were supported; full scalar invariance did not hold for all indicators, so we report separate within-group SEMs rather than a constrained multi-group model (see Supplemental Table S2 for details).
text.formatted: Configural and metric invariance were supported; full scalar invariance did not hold for all indicators, so we report separate within-group SEMs rather than a constrained multi-group model (see Supplemental Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S2</ref> for details).

text.text: Descriptive performance is summarized in Table 1.
text.formatted: Descriptive performance is summarized in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: As expected, Matching accuracy was substantially higher than DE accuracy across tasks and age groups.
DE performance showed substantial individual variation in both younger and older adults, with lower average accuracy in older adults.

Matching performance was near ceiling with considerably less variability, yet sufficient individual variation remained to define reliable latent factors: the total composite reliability of the matching indicators was high in both groups (ωt = .92 younger, .90 older), of which the general Matching factor captured a more modest share once reliable domain-specific Note.
All scores are on a 0-100 scale -the same values entered into the SEM.

Matching and delayed estimation values are accuracy scores [100 × (1 -mean angular error / 90°)]; the SSTM value is a pattern reproduction score (percentage match between the original and reproduced dot pattern after optimal alignment); updating and Gf values are percentage correct (updating: correctly recalled final values; reasoning tests: correct items).

For the matching and delayed estimation tasks, the value shown is the mean across the three trial-split parcels used as SEM indicators; because the parcels are random thirds of trials, their individual means do not differ meaningfully from this average, so per-parcel scores are not reported separately.
(color, orientation) variance is separated out (hierarchical ωH; see Figure 2).
text.formatted: (color, orientation) variance is separated out (hierarchical ωH; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Because the matching distributions deviated from normality at this ceiling level, robustness of all SEM results was confirmed with rank-normalized indicators (see Supplemental Materials for these results).
Correlation Models.

Model fit for the model estimating zero-order correlations among the general factors was acceptable for both groups (younger: PPP = .16, BCFI = .974, BRMSEA = .036, 95% CrI [.023, .048]; older: PPP = .60, BCFI = 1.000, BRMSEA = .004, 95% CrI [.000, .033]; see Table S1 for full fit statistics).

text.text: Study 2 used data from a large study investigating cognitive processes underlying individual differences in cognitive abilities.

3 The study comprised a battery of 28 tasks distributed across three in-laboratory sessions of approximately 3.5 hours each; the perceptual matching tasks were administered in the second session, and the WMC battery and intelligence assessment in the third.

Younger adults (N = 267; Mage = 23.0, SD = 3.6, range 18-35; 179 women, 80 men, 1 non-binary) were recruited via an online job market and mailing lists and received CHF 200 for the full study or partial course credit if they were students.
All participants provided written informed consent.

3 None of the analyses reported in this manuscript have been previously published from this dataset. Courage and Frischkorn (2026) reported results on the relation between processing speed and WMC from the same dataset but using only partially overlapping tasks from the study.

On each trial, target and probe were presented simultaneously on white  Study 2 Perceptual Matching Tasks.

Color matching (A, B) and luminance matching (C, D) were each administered in two spatial arrangements: side-by-side (A, C), with target and adjustable probe shown as two horizontally separated stimuli, and concentric (B, D), with the probe at the center of a target ring.

On each trial, after a fixation cross (400-600 ms) the target and probe appeared simultaneously and remained visible until response.

Participants first adjusted the probe to match the target by moving the cursor along the response wheel (color matching) or the linear response track (luminance matching) with no deadline on the matching response, then gave a confidence judgment, followed by an inter-trial interval (1,000-1,400 ms).
The two configurations are contrasted in the Matching Configuration Comparison.

On each trial, an array of 2 or 4 colored dots was presented for 1,000 ms, followed by a 1,000 ms blank retention interval; at test, a probe dot indicated one randomly selected memory item and participants reproduced its color on the same continuous color wheel as in the matching task, without a response deadline (100 trials; 50 at each memory load).
Performance was scored as reproduction accuracy [100 × (1 -mean angular error / 90°)], as in Study 1.

Latent-variable SEMs were estimated with Bayesian estimation as in Study 1, with standardized latent variances and bifactor structures in which specific factors are orthogonal to the general factors: domain-specific factors for color and luminance matching, as in Study 1, and task-specific method factors for the four WMCPM task types (see below).

To evaluate which tasks of the broader WMCPM battery captured most of the shared WMCPM variance compared to task-specific variance, we estimated the WMCPM factor with three parcels each from the complex span, letter updating, numerical updating, and color-binding tasks and introduced method factors for each task type (see the Supplementary Materials for detailed results).

As in Study 1, three parcels each from the color and luminance matching tasks served as indicators of the Matching bifactor, with a domainspecific factor per feature domain; in the main model these parcels pooled trials across the sideby-side and concentric arrangements (a configuration-separated model is reported under
The WMCDE factor also used three parcels aggregated across memory load as indicators.

Accuracy was scored as 100 × (1 -mean error / max error) for matching and WMCDE tasks; and percentage correct for WMCPM tasks.
As in Study 1, all accuracy indicators were placed on the common 0-100 metric, which here keeps their variances comparable to the raw IST-5 subtest scores that index Gf.

We again estimated three models : (1) a correlation model with all factors freely correlated, (2) a residual model in which both the WMCDE and WMCPM factors were simultaneously regressed on Matching, yielding residual correlations with Gf after accounting for variance shared with Matching, and (3) the reverse residual model in which Matching was regressed on both WMCPM and WMCDE, as in Study 1.

As Study 2 included younger adults only, all models were estimated for the full sample.

text.text: Table 3 reports zero-order and residual latent correlations with Gf and the corresponding proportional reductions in explained variance.

Matching accuracy accounted for a substantial and consistent share of both WMC factors' Gf-predictive variance across studies and age groups, with the largest reduction for WMCDE in older adults, despite the different WMCPM batteries used in Study 1 and Study 2.
The reverse residual models complete this picture with a marked evidential asymmetry.

WMCDE and WMCPM retained Gf-predictive variance beyond Matching in every group (smallest BF10 = 8.12), whereas Matching retained little credible Gf-predictive variance beyond its memory-enriched counterparts (WMCDE in Study 1; WMCPM and WMCDE jointly in Study 2; largest BF10 = 2.31), with inconclusive Bayes factors in all groups (Table 3, Matching rows, reports the corresponding proportional reductions).

An order-restriction test supported the asymmetry predicted by our assumption that Matching variance is contained in WMCDE variance: the reduction of the Matching-Gf relation was credibly larger than the reduction of the WM factors' jointly explained Gf variance, in Study 1 younger adults (Δ = .46, 95% CrI [.02, .80], BForder = 48.37) and in Study 2 (Δ = .49, 95% CrI [.20, .75], BForder > 100).

text.text: In older adults, where only WMCDE was available as a control, the same contrast was positive but inconclusive (Δ = .14, 95% CrI [-.32, .52], BForder = 2.55).

As all residual tests were performed at the latent level, where correlations are estimated free of attenuation by indicator unreliability, this asymmetry is not an artifact of differential measurement reliability.
We set out to decompose the WMC-Gf link into a component reflecting perceptual representation quality and a component specific to WM maintenance.
Perceptual matching, which requires no memory maintenance, accounted for a substantial share of the covarianceroughly 60-73% of WMCDE's Gf-related variance and about 45% of that of WMCPM (Table 3).
text.formatted: Perceptual matching, which requires no memory maintenance, accounted for a substantial share of the covarianceroughly 60-73% of WMCDE's Gf-related variance and about 45% of that of WMCPM (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: The two residual tests were asymmetric: WM maintenance retained a credible Gf-predictive contribution beyond Matching in every group, whereas controlling for the memory factors (WMCDE in Study 1; both WM factors in Study 2) reduced the Matching-Gf relation, leaving the evidence for a residual link inconclusive in all groups.
This pattern is consistent with Matching's
Gf-related variance being largely contained within that of WMC.
The maintenance-specific contribution to Gf held in both age groups, but perceptual matching accounted for a larger portion of WMCDE's Gf variance in older than younger adults.
This quantitative difference echoes the tightened coupling of sensory and intellectual functioning with adult age (Lindenberger & Baltes, 1994).
text.formatted: This quantitative difference echoes the tightened coupling of sensory and intellectual functioning with adult age <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lindenberger & Baltes, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: The association between perceptual matching and Gf has longstanding historical roots:

Galton (1883) proposed that sensory discrimination underlies general intelligence, Spearman (1904) could not confirm it convincingly with the methods of his era, but latent-variable studies later revived the conjecture (Deary et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Galton (1883) proposed that sensory discrimination underlies general intelligence, <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Spearman (1904)</ref> could not confirm it convincingly with the methods of his era, but latent-variable studies later revived the conjecture <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Deary et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Our matching tasks extend this line: Matching accuracy predicted Gf substantially in younger adults (r = .52/.56) and strongly in older adults (r = .71), despite imposing no retention interval.
This shared variance is not specific to the visual domain or to any shared stimulus content.

Matching-WMCPM correlations were r = .45 (Study 1, younger adults) and r = .45 (Study 2), even though the WMCPM tasks drew on spatial, verbal, and numerical content, and reasoning tests share no stimulus content with matching.
A common limit on the fidelity of representations, rather than shared task content, most parsimoniously explains why a maintenance-free perceptual task covaries with both memory and reasoning.

This is consistent with a global signal-to-noise ratio explaining general cognitive abilities (Oberauer et al., 2026) and with evidence that visual WM differences trace largely to a perceptual rather than mnemonic source (Pratte & Green, 2023).
text.formatted: This is consistent with a global signal-to-noise ratio explaining general cognitive abilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Oberauer et al., 2026)</ref> and with evidence that visual WM differences trace largely to a perceptual rather than mnemonic source <ref type="bibr">(Pratte & Green, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The present results are consistent with a signal-to-noise account but do not constitute direct evidence for it.
Behavioral Matching accuracy may also reflect motor noise, criterion setting, or strategic encoding, rather than a general signal-to-noise ratio.
These alternatives, however, offer no explanation for the strong correlation of matching with WMC and Gf.

Still, the covariance pattern cannot say which aspect of the signal-to-noise ratio is shared: a common level of noise or shared variance in signal strength both produce the same correlational signature.
Adjudicating between them requires an independent estimate of noise that does not depend on signal strength, which equivalent-noise paradigms provide (Lu & Dosher, 2008).
text.formatted: Adjudicating between them requires an independent estimate of noise that does not depend on signal strength, which equivalent-noise paradigms provide <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Lu & Dosher, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The Supplementary Materials elaborate on the specific assumptions underlying the decomposition.
Individual differences in WMC tasks are usually interpreted as differences in the capacity to maintain information.

Yet, unlike research on constructs such as attentional control (Engle, 2002), which isolates attention-control variance from other task-required processes (Rey-Mermet et al., 2025; von Bastian et al., 2020), WMC research has rarely isolated maintenance-specific variance from other influences on performance.
text.formatted: Yet, unlike research on constructs such as attentional control <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Engle, 2002)</ref>, which isolates attention-control variance from other task-required processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Rey-Mermet et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">von Bastian et al., 2020)</ref>, WMC research has rarely isolated maintenance-specific variance from other influences on performance.

text.text: The present design comes closer: Because the matching and DE tasks differ only in the requirement to hold multiple items in WM, the DE residual after partialling out Matching estimates maintenance-specific variance.
These residual correlations with Gf were credible across groups, indicating a maintenance-related contribution beyond perceptual precision.
How do these results relate to prior reports that WMC fully mediates the relationship between intelligence and sensory discrimination (Jastrzębski et al., 2021; Troche et al., 2014)?
text.formatted: How do these results relate to prior reports that WMC fully mediates the relationship between intelligence and sensory discrimination <ref type="bibr">(Jastrzębski et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Troche et al., 2014)</ref>?

text.text: Our reverse residual models put the same question to maintenance-free perceptual matching:
Matching retained no credible Gf variance beyond the memory factors (residual r = .17-.28, all Bayes factors inconclusive).

This is what one should expect if WMC tasks require forming precise representations and maintaining them, whereas matching requires only the former: A mediator containing all of a predictor's Gf-relevant variance, plus more, must mediate it fully.
Full mediation therefore carries no information about which construct is more fundamental, and does not license the conclusion that perceptual precision plays no explanatory role for intelligence.

Re-analysing the data of Jastrzębski et al. (2021) and Troche et al. (2014) (Supplementary Materials) reproduces this pattern; whether full mediation obtains depends on how broadly the mediator is measured.
text.formatted: Re-analysing the data of <ref type="bibr">Jastrzębski et al. (2021)</ref> and <ref type="bibr">Troche et al. (2014)</ref> (Supplementary Materials) reproduces this pattern; whether full mediation obtains depends on how broadly the mediator is measured.

text.text: By the same standard, the asymmetry we report licenses no primacy claim for perceptual precision either.
The same logic applies to a related argument by Tsukahara et al. (2020).
text.formatted: The same logic applies to a related argument by <ref type="bibr">Tsukahara et al. (2020)</ref>.

text.text: They reported that attentional control fully mediates the link between intelligence and sensory discrimination, whereas discrimination does not mediate the attentional-control-intelligence link.
They interpreted this asymmetry as attention control being the more fundamental construct.
If attention-control tasks depend on all the discrimination measures' Gf-related variance plus more, that mediation must occur without establishing causal priority.

For Matching and DE, the experimental manipulation of the maintenance demand justifies the assumption that DE variance fully contains Matching variance; for discrimination and attention control we can only rely on plausibility.

We find it plausible that perceptual precision contributes to every task involving stimulus discrimination, as all attention-control measures do, and less plausible that attention control matters in discrimination or matching tests, as they don't involve strong distractors or misleading response tendencies (Oberauer, 2024).
text.formatted: We find it plausible that perceptual precision contributes to every task involving stimulus discrimination, as all attention-control measures do, and less plausible that attention control matters in discrimination or matching tests, as they don't involve strong distractors or misleading response tendencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Oberauer, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The present results are also relevant for accounts of the positive manifold underlying the g factor.
Process Overlap Theory (POT, Kovacs & Conway, 2016) holds that g is not a causal entity but an emergent index of overlapping domain-general executive processes sampled by diverse tests.
text.formatted: Process Overlap Theory (POT, <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Kovacs & Conway, 2016)</ref> holds that g is not a causal entity but an emergent index of overlapping domain-general executive processes sampled by diverse tests.

text.text: A task minimizing executive demands should then predict Gf only weakly.

Yet our Matching -with no distractors, no conflicting goals, and no retention interval -predicted Gf substantially, and correlated sizably with WMC batteries drawing on spatial, verbal, and numerical content (r = .45 and .45), although POT predicts near-zero correlations between tests that share few executive processes.
Accommodating this within POT requires assuming that Matching itself taps executive processes, stretching the concept until it becomes allencompassing.

A signal-to-noise-ratio account offers a better explanation: A global limit on representational fidelity constraining perceptual encoding and WM maintenance alike would act as a genuine common cause of the positive manifold (Oberauer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A signal-to-noise-ratio account offers a better explanation: A global limit on representational fidelity constraining perceptual encoding and WM maintenance alike would act as a genuine common cause of the positive manifold <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Oberauer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Four limitations deserve acknowledgment.

First, we cannot fully rule out a contribution of motivation to the Matching-Gf association; a motivation account would, however, have to explain why the least demanding task carries substantial variance shared with Gf.
Plausible motivational effects on performance are modest: ≈ 9% of variance, from a motivationperformance correlation of r ≈ .30 (Gignac, 2018).
text.formatted: Plausible motivational effects on performance are modest: ≈ 9% of variance, from a motivationperformance correlation of r ≈ .30 <ref type="bibr">(Gignac, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Second, both samples are predominantly White, Swiss, and university-educated (a WEIRD population; Henrich et al., 2010), limiting generalization; the age comparison is cross-sectional, so age differences are confounded with cohort.
text.formatted: Second, both samples are predominantly White, Swiss, and university-educated (a WEIRD population; <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Henrich et al., 2010)</ref>, limiting generalization; the age comparison is cross-sectional, so age differences are confounded with cohort.

text.text: Third, we examined perceptual precision only for visual features (color, orientation, and luminance); generalization to other domains remains open.
Fourth, the analyses were not preregistered: the decomposition models were specified after data collection, making the model comparisons exploratory rather than confirmatory.
The convergence of results across the two studies, rather than any single prespecified test, carries the evidential weight.
The Supplementary Materials contain an extended discussion of each limitation.

A large part of the variance shared between WMC and Gf is also shared with a measure of perceptual precision that requires no memory maintenance and little, if any, attention control, a pattern that held across content domains and is consistent with a general signal-to-noise ratio limit on representational fidelity constraining cognition from perception to memory to reasoning.

At the same time, WM maintenance makes an additional contribution to fluid intelligence, providing stronger support than previous research to the hypothesis that the limited capacity of WM contributes to variance in intelligence.

For each study and age group we estimated three structurally equivalent latent models.
The correlation model freely estimates the latent correlations among the perceptual matching, delayed estimation, working-memory capacity, and intelligence factors.

The residual model regresses delayed estimation (WMCDE) -and, where the design permits, WMCPM -on matching accuracy, isolating the variance these factors do not share with perceptual matching in the latent residuals (i.e., disturbances).

The reverse residual model regresses matching on both WMCPM and delayed estimation (Study 1 younger adults, Study 2) or on delayed estimation alone (Study 1 older adults, where no separate WMCPM factor was identified), isolating the variance matching does not share with the WMC factors.
Because the three models are algebraic reparameterisations of the same covariance structure, they have identical global fit; Table S1 therefore reports this shared fit once per group.

All models use parallel-test constraints (equal loadings and equal error variances within each parcel bundle), theoretically justified for random trial-split parcels and favored by approximate leave-one-out cross-validation over unconstrained variants in all three groups (ΔLOOIC = -23, -49, and -33 for S1 Younger, S1 Older, and S2, respectively; negative values favor the constrained model).

Because the primary Study 1 analyses report separate within-group structural models for younger and older adults, we tested whether the measurement model is invariant across age groups, using the standard configural → metric → scalar sequence, estimated with Bayesian multi-group CFA as in all other analyses (indicators z-scored on the combined sample, so that group differences in means and variances are preserved).
Invariance steps were compared via the change in Bayesian fit indices and via approximate leave-one-out/WAIC cross-validation differences.

The model specified one factor per task domain -color matching, orientation matching, color delayed estimation, and orientation delayed estimation -together with a fluidintelligence factor indicated by the three reasoning tests and the two WMCPM tasks.

The WMCPM tasks are modelled as part of the Gf factor here because in older adults WMCPM and Gf are empirically inseparable (a separately estimated WMCPM factor yields a latent correlation above one and a non-positive-definite solution); a common, proper model across groups therefore requires WMCPM to load on Gf, as in the primary older-adult model.
Configural invariance held, with good fit in both groups (Table S2).

The measurement model decomposes matching and DE into a general accuracy factor and domain-specific factors.

For matching, a general Match factor loads on all colour-and orientation-matching parcels, while domain-specific MatC and MatO factors capture the residual variance specific to each feature domain; delayed estimation is modelled analogously (general DE plus domain-specific DeC and DeO).
The WMCPM and Gf factors load directly on their task scores (WMC tasks and reasoning tests, respectively), without a parcel structure.
Each matching and DE task is split into three parcels by randomly partitioning its trials.

Because these parcels are drawn from the same pool of equivalent trials, they are treated as parallel measurements: Their loadings are constrained to be equal (tau-equivalence) and their residual variances are constrained to be equal (the parallel-test model).

text.text: After rank normalization, the latent correlation between Matching accuracy and Gf was r = .51 (S1 Younger) and r = .71 (S1 Older), closely mirroring the untransformed estimates (r = .52 and r = .71, respectively).

Matching accuracy continued to account for a comparable share of delayed estimation's Gf-predictive variance (rank-normalised proportional reduction: 63% in younger adults, 68% in older adults), consistent with the primary analysis and supporting the robustness of the main findings to violations of multivariate normality.

This check also bears on a second concern: to the extent that matching accuracy approaches ceiling to different degrees in the two age groups, the raw accuracy scale could compress individual differences differentially across groups.

Rank normalization removes any monotone distortion of the score scale, including ceiling compression, so the essentially unchanged latent correlations and proportional reductions indicate that the age-group pattern -including the stronger Matching-Gf association in older adults -is not an artifact of differential scale compression.
A rank-normalisation robustness check was not conducted for Study 2, as the primary results showed no evidence of distributional problems in that sample.

Reanalysis of Published Datasets The containment account makes a prediction about other studies: Whether a construct X fully mediates the sensory discrimination-Gf relation should depend on how broadly the task battery for measuring X samples Gf-relevant processes.
The share of the X-Gf covariance accounted for by discrimination should be substantial wherever discrimination and Gf are strongly related.

We tested this in the publicly available person-level data of Jastrzębski et al. (2021) (https://osf.io/xp6g8/) and Tsukahara et al. text.text: This comparison underscores that conclusions based on partial versus full mediation are unstable across studies that measure constructs with different batteries of indicators.
They are not diagnostic of causal priority.
The following extends the brief limitations discussion in the main text.
Motivational confounds.

Stable individual differences in motivation or effort could in principle generate spurious correlations among cognitive tasks if higher-motivated individuals consistently perform better across all measures.
However, two features of the present data weigh against a strong motivational account.
Structurally, an effort account would have to explain why the least demanding task (i.e. matching, with no WM demand) shows the strongest Gf correlation in older adults.

Statistically, the plausible upper bound of motivation's influence can be estimated: the latent correlation between conscientiousness (a proxy for effortful engagement) and intelligence is approximately r ≈ .30 (Gignac, 2018), placing the maximum shared variance from motivation at roughly 9%, far less than the 45-73% of the WMC-Gf and DE-Gf covariance attributable to perceptual-matching accuracy in the present studies.
text.formatted: Statistically, the plausible upper bound of motivation's influence can be estimated: the latent correlation between conscientiousness (a proxy for effortful engagement) and intelligence is approximately r ≈ .30 <ref type="bibr">(Gignac, 2018)</ref>, placing the maximum shared variance from motivation at roughly 9%, far less than the 45-73% of the WMC-Gf and DE-Gf covariance attributable to perceptual-matching accuracy in the present studies.

text.text: Although the matching task involves no WM retention interval, the accuracy score, computed from the mean angular reproduction error, aggregates multiple sources of variability beyond sensory signal-to-noise.

Motor noise in the continuous adjustment response, response criterion-setting, occasional attentional lapses, and potentially strategic encoding of the target (e.g., verbally labeling a color) all contribute to matching error.
These contributions are not WM maintenance processes, but they are also not exclusively reflections of the sensory signal-to-noise ratio.
The present results therefore cannot constitute direct evidence for the signal-to-noise-ratio account of general intelligence; they are consistent with it.

A further consequence is that the proportional reductions reported in the main text are lower bounds on the proportion of the WMC-Gf link that is shared with perceptual precision: To the extent that matching error contains Gf-irrelevant motor and criterion variance, the shared perceptual component is underestimated (see Conditions for the Decomposition Interpretation above).

Future work using forced-choice discrimination tasks (which eliminate the motor adjustment component) or similarity judgment tasks (which do not depend on precise motor responses) will provide cleaner indices of perceptual precision.
We examined continuous feature spaces: color hue and orientation (Study 1), and luminance (Study 2).

The bifactor model in Study 2 supports domaingenerality across these three dimensions (variance in matching accuracy that cuts across color, luminance, and orientation predicts Gf), but it remains open whether equivalent patterns emerge for other continuous feature spaces (e.g., spatial frequency, motion direction, pitch, duration).
Perceptual matching (adjusting a continuous probe to match a target with no delay) is one operationalization of a maintenance-free perceptual task.

Other zerodelay paradigms such as forced-choice discrimination (which stimulus is higher in contrast?) or simultaneous similarity judgment (how similar are these two colors?) eliminate the motor adjustment component and may yield purer estimates of perceptual discrimination.
Whether these paradigms yield equivalent individual-difference structure is addressed in follow-up work in our lab.

The matching paradigm also requires sustained encoding of the target while the probe is adjusted; gaze shifts between target and probe could recruit brief iconic storage, and whether this constitutes a form of early WM is debated (Pratte & Green, 2023).

Two features of these matrices motivate the structural models.
First, the indicators form a positive manifold: with negligible exceptions, all correlations are positive.
Second, the perceptual matching indicators (MatC, MatO, MatL) correlate not only with the delayedestimation and working-memory indicators but also with the fluid-intelligence indicators.

This is the raw-data pattern that the latent models subsequently formalise and disattenuate for measurement error, allowing the perceptual and maintenance contributions to the WMC-Gf relationship to be partitioned.

the covariance of Gf with other constructs: 68% and 38% of the WM-Gf covariance in Jastrzębski's Studies 1 and 2, 81% and 50% of the WMC-Gf covariance in Tsukahara's Studies 1 and 2, and 92% and 66% of their AC-Gf covariance -bracketing the correlations between Gf and perceptual matching in our studies.

Second, whether or not a mediating construct (WMC or AC) fully mediated the link between sensory discrimination and Gf depended on how broad the test battery for measuring the mediating construct was.

Full mediation was obtained with Jastrzębski's WM batteries (in their Study 2 the residual was nominally negative, r = -.23, 95% CrI [-.48, -.02], indicating no positive unique path from discrimination to Gf) and with Tsukahara's AC factors.
By contrast, sensory discrimination retained clear unique variance beyond a WMC factor formed from the three complex span tasks in both of Tsukahara's studies (r = .32 and .33, BF10 > 100 in both).

text.text: We argue that this is a consequence of the relatively narrow measurement of WMC through only one task paradigm -complex span batteries do not exhaust the shared variance between Gf and sensory discrimination.
Two qualifications apply:

First, battery breadth was not operationalized independently of these outcomes, and broader batteries also contain more indicators, so higher reliability of the mediating factor is an alternative explanation that these analyses cannot rule out.

Second, these reanalyses are descriptive and use simplified measurement models; they are reported to illustrate that the decomposition question and the mediation question give different answers in the same data, not as re-estimates of the original studies' models.
One final observation: In Tsukahara's Study 1, the link between Gf and AC was largely mediated by sensory discrimination (proportional reduction 92%; residual r = .21, BF10 = 1.61, inconclusive).

Applying the same mediation logic that these authors used to declare AC the causally fundamental construct would, in light of this result, have crowned sensory discrimination as the more fundamental construct.

Luminance Matching.
On each trial, target and probe gray patches were presented simultaneously in side-by-side or concentric arrangement, with gray levels spanning 10-90 on a 0-100 lightness scale.

Participants adjusted the probe's grayscale value by moving the mouse cursor along a linear response track below the stimuli until a mouse click confirmed the match, followed by a confidence judgment (20 trials per condition, 40 total).
Performance was scored on the same 0-100 accuracy scale as color matching [100 × (1 -mean error / max error)], with deviation computed on the response scale.

Figure4 verbal/numerical tasks and one visual binding task.

In the Number Complex Span task, participants selected the larger of two two-digit numbers on each of 4 steps (2,000 ms per comparison) while memorizing the number indicated by a directional arrow after each selection, then serially recalled all 4 memorized numbers at test (12 trials; scored as percentage recalled in order).

In the Letter Updating task, participants encoded 4 color-letter bindings, updated 2 of them by replacing the bound letter with a new one, then recalled the current letter for each color via a response matrix (1,500 ms per encoded and updated item; 10-s recall deadline; 15 trials; scored as percentage of correctly recalled final letters).

In the Number Updating task, participants encoded 4-5 digits at distinct grid locations in a 4 × 4 grid, applied three successive arithmetic operations per trial, each to a randomly selected digit, so that some digits were updated more than once and others not at all (+1, +2, -1, or -2; 1,000 ms per encoding, update, and retention interval), and recalled the final digit at each location by key press (16 trials; scored as percentage correct).

In the Color Binding task, participants encoded the color and location of 4-5 items presented one at a time in a 4 × 4 grid (1,000 ms per item; 1,000 ms retention), then recalled either the color at a probed location or the location of a probed color via cued recall (16 trials; scored as percentage correct).

Regressing Matching on WMCPM alone yielded a similar residual (r = .21, 95% CrI [.05, .38], BF10 = 3.31, at the boundary of the inconclusive band), whereas controlling for WMCDE alone left a credible residual (r = .29, 95% CrI [.12, .46], BF10 = 22.38).
The single colour DE task does not fully account for all the shared variance between Matching and Gf (both model variants are reported in more detail in the Supplementary Materials).

Taken together, Study 2 replicates the Study 1 pattern: Matching accounts for a large share of the WMCPM-Gf and WMCDE-Gf relationships, with WM maintenance contributing a residual Gf-predictive component.
The residual path coefficients are illustrated in Figure6.

Matching Configuration Comparison.Study 2 presented color and luminance matching in two configurations: side-by-side (target and probe simultaneously visible with horizontal separation) and concentric (probe in the middle of a target ring, reducing eye movement demands; see Figure4).

To test whether the Matching-Gf association depends on the spatial arrangement, we re-fit the behavioral SEM with configuration-specific parcels (3 per configuration × feature domain) in two forms: one in which all matching parcels load on a single Matching factor, and one in which the side-by-side and
